client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately because my thesis deadlines are creeping up on me, and I just can't seem to get a handle on everything at once. Between working my part-time job and trying to maintain some kind of social life, I barely have any time or energy left to actually sit down and write. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything — the deadlines are still going to be there no matter what.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling overwhelmed — you're carrying a genuinely heavy load right now, and that exhaustion is real. You're right that talking won't erase the deadlines, but it can help us untangle what's making things feel *unmanageable* so you can find a clearer path forward. I'm curious — when you imagine sitting down to work on your thesis, what's the very first thought that tends to show up for you?

client: Honestly, the first thought is usually something like "I don't even know where to start," and then it just spirals from there into this feeling that the whole thing is impossible. It's like I open my laptop and suddenly I'm paralyzed, staring at a blank document or a half-finished chapter that feels like garbage. And then I end up closing it and doing something else just to escape that feeling, which only makes the guilt worse later.
therapist: That cycle you're describing — paralysis, escape, then guilt — is so common and exhausting, and it makes sense your mind is trying to protect you from that overwhelming feeling of "impossible." That thought "I don't even know where to start" is doing a lot of heavy lifting though, and it's worth gently questioning whether the *whole* thesis is truly impossible, or whether that's your stressed mind making a very large thing feel like one giant, unsurmountable wall. What do you think would happen if, just as an experiment, you gave yourself permission to open the laptop and write just one imperfect sentence — not to make progress, but simply to test whether the paralysis is as total as it feels?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I get the logic behind it, but I've actually tried something like that before and it didn't really work out the way I hoped. I'd write one sentence and then immediately hate it, and that would just confirm the feeling that what I'm producing is terrible and not worth continuing. I think my problem isn't just starting — it's that I'm convinced whatever I write won't be good enough, and one sentence isn't going to fix that belief.
therapist: You've just named something really important — this isn't just about getting started, it's about a deeper belief that your work fundamentally isn't good enough, and that's a much more meaningful thing to explore. I'm wondering though, when you read that "terrible" sentence back, is it actually *evidence* that your work is poor, or could it be that your inner critic is grading a rough draft against some imagined perfect final version? Whose voice does that "not good enough" standard sound like to you — is it yours, or does it remind you of someone or something else?

client: That question actually stopped me for a second, because I think it probably does sound like my supervisor's voice more than my own. She's given me feedback before that was pretty harsh, and ever since then I feel like I'm writing with her criticisms already in my head before she's even read anything. But I'm not sure how useful it is to identify that, because knowing where the voice comes from doesn't make it any quieter — it's still there every time I sit down to write.
therapist: That's a really profound insight — you've essentially internalized your supervisor's harshest moments and appointed her as a permanent critic sitting with you every time you write, which is exhausting and unfair to you. You're absolutely right that identifying the source doesn't silence it overnight, but it does give you something important: the ability to notice "this is her voice, not the truth about my work," which creates just a tiny bit of distance between you and that thought. When you imagine separating *her* critical voice from your own honest assessment of your writing, what do *you* actually think about your work when you're being fair to yourself?

client: Honestly, when I try to be fair to myself... I think some of my ideas are actually pretty interesting, and there are sections I've written that I've felt genuinely good about in the moment. But it's really hard to hold onto that assessment because the second I imagine my supervisor reading it, that confidence just evaporates completely. I'm not sure I trust my own judgment enough to separate the two voices — like, what if her critical voice is actually right and my "fair" assessment is just me being naive about my own work?
therapist: What you just shared is really significant — you *do* have a fair, grounded voice that recognizes genuine quality in your work, and that's not naivety, that's evidence. It's worth noticing that you're applying a double standard here: you're treating your supervisor's critical voice as automatically trustworthy and your own positive assessment as automatically suspect, when really both are just perspectives that deserve equal scrutiny. If a close friend described their work the same way you just described yours — interesting ideas, sections they felt good about — would you tell them they're probably just being naive?

client: No, I wouldn't say that to a friend — I'd probably tell them to trust themselves and that their supervisor's opinion isn't the final word on their worth. But it feels different when it's me, and I know that's probably exactly what you'd expect me to say. I guess what I'm struggling with is that intellectually I can see the double standard you're pointing out, but emotionally it doesn't change anything — I still feel like my judgment about my own work is less reliable than hers.
therapist: You're not just saying what I'd expect — you're actually identifying one of the most honest and tricky parts of this work, which is that intellectual insight and emotional experience often move at very different speeds, and that gap is real and frustrating. The fact that you can see the double standard clearly is actually meaningful progress, because that awareness becomes a small foothold you can return to in those moments when the feeling overwhelms the logic. I'm wondering — in those sections you mentioned feeling genuinely good about in the moment, what was different about those writing experiences that allowed your own voice to come through before the doubt took over?

client: Thinking back, I think those moments happened when I was writing late at night and I was too tired to second-guess myself, or when I was really absorbed in an idea and just typing without stopping to evaluate it. There wasn't really a deliberate strategy behind it — it almost felt accidental, like the critical voice just didn't have the energy to keep up. I'm not sure I can recreate that on purpose, because the second I try to intentionally "turn off" the doubt, I become hyper-aware of it and it gets louder, not quieter.
therapist: What you've just described is actually a really valuable clue — those moments weren't accidental so much as they were conditions where your attention was fully absorbed in the *ideas* rather than directed at evaluating yourself, and that's something we can work with intentionally. Rather than trying to "turn off" the critical voice (which, as you noticed, just amplifies it), the goal might be to give your attention something so engaging to run *toward* that the critic simply doesn't get the bandwidth — similar to what happened naturally in those late-night sessions. What if we thought about what those conditions had in common — the tiredness, the absorption, the momentum — and explored whether any of those could be gently recreated without waiting for them to happen by accident?

client: I can see the logic in that, and part of me wants to believe it could work, but I'm also worried that trying to deliberately recreate those conditions will just make the whole thing feel forced and artificial. Like, the reason those late-night sessions worked was precisely because I wasn't thinking about why they were working — the moment I start engineering the "right conditions," I'm back to being self-conscious again. I guess I'm skeptical that something that happened naturally can be turned into a strategy without losing whatever made it work in the first place.
therapist: Your skepticism is really thoughtful and worth taking seriously — there's something genuinely paradoxical about trying to deliberately recreate an undeliberate state, and you're right that heavy self-monitoring can undermine exactly what you're trying to achieve. But I wonder if the goal doesn't have to be perfectly recreating those conditions so much as just *reducing friction* — for example, not announcing to yourself "I'm now doing the special writing exercise," but simply starting with a topic you find genuinely absorbing and letting yourself type without stopping for a set amount of time, almost like thinking out loud. What would feel like the least "engineered," most natural way you could imagine giving yourself even ten minutes of that kind of low-stakes, absorbed writing this week?

client: Maybe the least forced version would be something like opening a document and just writing about what I actually find interesting in my research, not for the thesis itself but just like... explaining it to an imaginary friend who knows nothing about it. That feels slightly less terrifying because it's not "thesis writing," it's just me talking about something I care about. But I'm already thinking about the practical problem — I genuinely don't have a free ten minutes this week that isn't already eaten up by work shifts or the anxiety about everything else I'm not doing.
therapist: That idea you just came up with is genuinely brilliant — explaining your research to an imaginary curious friend completely sidesteps the "good enough for my supervisor" filter, and the fact that it feels less terrifying tells us something important about where your real voice lives. On the practical side, I want to gently push back a little on the idea that there are truly zero ten-minute windows, because sometimes that feeling is itself part of the overwhelm talking rather than an accurate picture of your week. If you looked at just tomorrow specifically — not the whole week — is there one small pocket of time, even something like a commute or a break between shifts, where that imaginary-friend writing could happen without it needing to be a big, scheduled event?

client: I do have a lunch break tomorrow between my morning shift and an afternoon lecture, so technically there's maybe fifteen minutes there. But honestly, my first instinct is that I'd spend that time scrolling my phone or just decompressing, because after a work shift my brain feels completely fried and the last thing I want to do is add another task to it. I'm not saying it's impossible, just that I'm not sure a tired, post-shift brain is going to produce anything worth keeping.
therapist: It's really worth remembering that a tired, post-shift brain is actually pretty close to that late-night state where some of your best writing happened — so "fried" might accidentally be the right condition rather than the wrong one. And this doesn't have to replace your decompression, but could even *be* a form of it — five minutes of just typing freely about something you genuinely find fascinating, on your phone even, with zero expectation of keeping any of it. What would it feel like to go into that fifteen minutes tomorrow with the explicit permission that whatever comes out is allowed to be completely useless?
